Élections fédérales : que proposent les: Federal election: what are the parties offering Indigenous peoples?
À l'approche du vote de demain, on se pe: With tomorrow's vote just around the corner, we look at the promises political parties have made to Indigenous peoples.
À l’occasion de ces élections fédérales,: With this federal election, I wanted to take stock of the promises the parties have made to Indigenous peoples. Through my work at APTN News, and as a Métis person, I know that Indigenous priorities are wide-ranging and diverse. The relationship between the federal government and Indigenous nations is made up of a web of treaties, constitutional frameworks, laws and agreements – and the Canadian government doesn’t always hold up its end of the bargain. Indigenous issues were not a central theme in the leaders’ debates, and most party platforms were only released as the voting period drew near. So I pulled together the scattered information I was able to obtain on the promises made to Canada’s Indigenous nations.
Certaines de ces promesses ne sont pas a: Some of these promises don’t come with specific financial commitments, but I include the investments being considered where the information is available.
À l'approche du vote de demain, on se pe: With tomorrow's vote just around the corner, we look at the promises political parties have made to Indigenous peoples. Here is what the Liberals, Conservatives, the New Democratic Party (NDP), the Bloc Québécois and the Green Party are offering Indigenous voters.
Le chef du Parti libéral, Mark Carney, s: Liberal Party leader Mark Carney wants to expand oil and gas production in Canada, notably by speeding up the construction of oil and gas pipelines. Although he has committed to consulting and partnering with the Indigenous peoples affected by energy resource projects, Mr. Carney has not specified whether Indigenous consent will be required for these projects.
Sous le mandat de Justin Trudeau, le gou: Under Justin Trudeau, the Liberal government passed <l1>the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) Act</l1>, which means Canadian legal decisions must respect UNDRIP, including by requiring the free, prior and informed consent of Indigenous peoples for projects taking place on their territories. That did not stop the Trudeau government from sending <l2>RCMP officers</l2> to arrest and forcibly remove Wet’suwet’en people who opposed the construction of the Coastal GasLink pipeline on their territory.
La <l1>plateforme électorale des libérau: The <l1>Liberal election platform</l1> speaks of the need for Indigenous participation and partnership in major infrastructure and resource development projects. Mark Carney would allocate an additional $250 million a year to the <l2>Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program</l2>, the federal government fund that lets Indigenous communities and businesses borrow money at lower interest rates to invest in projects on their territories.
Les libéraux créeraient également un nou: The Liberals would also create a new fund to support career development training and education ($100 million over four years), in the hope of increasing the number of doctors, teachers and builders from First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities, among others, and would increase post-secondary education funding for Indigenous students ($79 million in 2025-2026 and $29 million in 2026-2027).
En matière de conservation et de gestion: When it comes to conservation and environmental stewardship, the Liberals would give more funding to Indigenous Guardians. They plan to allocate an additional $10 million a year to that program, add 50 new Arctic Indigenous Guardians and create an Indigenous climate change preparedness and adaptation fund ($250 million).
L’administration Trudeau s’était engagée: The Trudeau administration had pledged to end all long-term boil-water advisories in communities by 2021. Today, <l1>33 communities</l1> still do not have access to safe drinking water. Although there is no new funding dedicated to ending the advisories, the Carney government wants to pass a law “affirming that First Nations have a human right to clean drinking water.” The Liberal election platform also states that they are committed to working with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities to build essential infrastructure through an investment of $2.5 billion.
Dans ce qui pourrait être un pas vers la: In what could be a step toward land back, the Liberals also want to “increase the lands added to reserves over the next four years.” There are no details on a timeline or on which First Nations would be consulted as part of this process.
Bien que les libéraux n’aient pas répond: Although the Liberals did not answer the question of whether they would increase funding for Indigenous media, they have committed to “strengthen the mandate of CBC/Radio-Canada” to include more Indigenous perspectives. CBC is home to <l1>CBC Indigenous</l1>, and Radio-Canada has <l2>Espaces autochtones</l2>, both dedicated to Indigenous reporting. The public broadcaster also produces Indigenous entertainment programming. The Liberals have pledged to increase CBC/Radio-Canada’s funding by $150 million a year for four years and to make the broadcaster’s funding “statutory,” meaning the approval of all of Parliament would be needed to cut CBC/Radio-Canada’s funding.

Carney affirme qu’il nouera des parte: Mr. Carney says he will forge partnerships with northern Indigenous leaders to strengthen <l1>Canada’s security in the Arctic</l1> through an increased Canadian Armed Forces presence. He has also pledged to invest in northern infrastructure, including housing, hydroelectricity, railways and highways. The Liberals intend to allocate $500 million a year over the next four years to “build the Arctic.”
Sous M. Trudeau, plusieurs commissions s: Under Mr. Trudeau, several commissions on Indigenous issues led to the development of the following “action plans”: <l1>the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s calls to action</l1>, the national action plan for <l2>missing and murdered Indigenous women, girls and 2SLGBTQIA+ people</l2> and the <l3>United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples action plan</l3>. While progress has been made on the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s calls to action, the other two have seen no movement. The Liberals say they will implement all three plans under Mark Carney’s leadership.
Les libéraux affirment qu’ils augmentero: The Liberals say they will also increase investments in Indigenous mental health, healing and wellness centres, and friendship centres. Although they have not specified how much funding could be allocated, it could be included in their health care and infrastructure spending.

Pierre Poilievre souhaite « libérer » le: Pierre Poilievre wants to “unleash” Canada’s oil and gas. His party would create a single window for issuing permits for resource extraction and infrastructure projects. Mr. Poilievre has repeatedly said that <l1>Bill C-69</l1> stands in the way of dozens of resource development projects and that, if elected, he will scrap it. However, that bill puts an emphasis on certain things, including environmental impact and Indigenous consultation before federal regulators issue permits for resource extraction projects.
Alors que, sur leur plateforme électoral: While the Conservatives’ election platform commits to “establishing a nation-to-nation consultation process for major laws and projects that directly affect First Nations, Inuit and Métis,” Mr. Poilievre has cut the permit approval timeline to one year, including assessment and consultation processes.
Pierre Poilievre s’est engagé à accélére: Pierre Poilievre has pledged to speed up development of the Ring of Fire, a mineral-rich region in northern Ontario, and has said he would approve all pending federal permits for projects in the region. First Nations leaders have said that <l1>this promise disregards Indigenous rights</l1>.
S’adressant à l’Assemblée des Premières: Speaking to the Assembly of First Nations, <l1>Mr. Poilievre said</l1> that “the Conservative Party supports the goals and aspirations of UNDRIP, but the Liberals’ proposal to ensure Canadian legislation respects UNDRIP raises questions about the legal meaning of free, prior and informed consent.” The Conservatives have opposed UNDRIP in the past, <l2>fearing that Indigenous peoples would gain a “veto” over projects carried out on their lands</l2>. Their 2025 platform does not mention UNDRIP
En cas de victoire, le parti compte mett: If they win, the party plans to implement <l1>the First Nations Resource Charge,</l1> which would allow companies to pay a portion of their taxes directly to First Nations. That way, the revenue would not be sent to Ottawa, and First Nations would not have to negotiate to get a share of the revenue from projects carried out on their lands. The initiative is supported by the <l2>First Nations Tax Commission</l2>.
Pierre Poilievre soutiendrait également: Pierre Poilievre would also support the creation of a Canadian Indigenous investment corporation ($11 million a year over four years) to inject capital into resource and industry projects, modelled on the <l1>Alberta Indigenous Opportunities Corporation</l1>.
En ce qui concerne le logement et les in: On housing and infrastructure, the Conservatives also plan to establish a “permanent stream of infrastructure funding for First Nations” and provide funding for Indigenous-led housing solutions. The Conservatives promise to ensure that funds go directly to communities, not to third-party consultants. They also want to allocate $50 million a year over two years to an “Indigenous Advancement Fund,” which would support measurable, community-led solutions to improve their lives.
Les conservateurs se sont également enga: The Conservatives have also pledged $25 million to fund Indigenous media. They are the only party to have made a commitment on this issue. However, they also intend to cut funding to CBC (while maintaining it for Radio-Canada), which has an <l1>Indigenous news service</l1> and produces Indigenous programming.
Les conservateurs veulent construire une: The Conservatives want to build a permanent military base in the Arctic, in Iqaluit, and a naval base in Churchill, Manitoba. They also want to build an Arctic security corridor between Yellowknife (N.W.T.) and Grays Bay (Nunavut). The corridor would include a 600-km all-season road between Yellowknife and Grays Bay.

Le <l1>NPD affirme</l1> qu’il ratifiera: The <l1>NDP says</l1> it will ratify UNDRIP and plans to “replace mere consultation with a standard of free, prior and informed consent, including for all decisions affecting constitutionally protected land rights, such as energy project assessments.” It intends to negotiate nation to nation with First Nations, Métis and Inuit.
<l1>S’adressant à l’Assemblée des Premiè: <l1>Speaking to the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) on April 23, Mr. Singh promised</l1> to respond to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 calls to action and the Working Group on Migration Management’s calls for justice. The NDP will also provide long-term funding for the search for graves at former residential schools and will table a bill to combat residential school denialism.
Le NPD affirme qu’il mettra fin aux avis: The NDP says it will end boil-water advisories on reserves and invest in Indigenous-led water management training programs. It will also invest in increasing health care, mental health and addiction resources in communities.
Comme les libéraux, le NPD s’engage à au: Like the Liberals, the NDP is committed to increasing CBC/Radio-Canada’s funding by $150 million a year, but does not commit to funding Indigenous-owned media.
Le parti affirme en outre qu’il élaborer: The party also says it will develop the <l1>Arctic and Northern Policy Framework</l1> in collaboration with Inuit to address the lack of infrastructure in northern communities. The NDP plans to invest <l2>$2 billion annually</l2> over four years in Indigenous housing and infrastructure, including by answering Nunavut’s call to build 3,000 homes by 2030.
Les habitants des régions isolées, en pa: People living in remote regions, particularly First Nations and Inuit in the North, <l1>have faced very high food prices for years</l1>. The NDP promises to introduce emergency price caps on basic food items, such as pasta, frozen vegetables and baby formula. It also wants to set up a code of conduct for grocery stores, give the Competition Bureau the job of monitoring grocery prices and impose penalties on grocers who charge higher prices. The NDP also wants to “fix” the <l2>Nutrition North Canada</l2> program, which provides subsidies to food retailers and community food programs in northern Canada, so that more food subsidies go into people’s pockets rather than corporations’. It also wants to permanently remove the GST on essentials such as prepared meals, diapers and Internet services.
Le NPD lancera une enquête nationale sur: The NDP will launch a national inquiry into systemic violence and racism against Indigenous peoples within Canadian institutions. Finally, unlike most police forces, First Nations police are not considered an “essential service,” so their funding is more precarious. Across the country, <l1>First Nations</l1> <l2>in Canada</l2> are loudly calling for funding equivalent to that of non-Indigenous police services. Mr. Singh said he would make First Nations policing an essential service and give it long-term funding.
Le Parti vert veut améliorer la particip: The Green Party wants to improve Indigenous participation in decision-making on industrial projects, respect the principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and legislate revenue sharing with First Nations to ensure they receive a portion of the profits from the development of their territories. The party does not want new oil and gas projects and intends to shift to renewable energy. The Greens have only released a <l1>partially costed platform</l1>, so not all of these initiatives have a budget listed in their election platform.
Le parti souhaite également favoriser l’: The party also wants to promote lithium mining and electric vehicle production in Canada. <l1>Many</l1> <l2>Indigenous</l2> <l3>groups</l3> oppose lithium mining on their territories because the process can be harmful to the environment. At a news conference, Jonathan Pedneault, co-leader of the Green Party of Canada, said his party would strengthen environmental regulations on mining and that any company wanting access to Canada’s resources would first have to obtain the free and informed consent of the affected Indigenous nations and local communities.
Les Verts souhaitent en outre financer l: The Greens also want to fund Indigenous-led protection of old-growth and boreal forests and increase Indigenous participation in environmental monitoring. They have also said they would increase funding for Indigenous-run education programs, including those related to Indigenous languages and knowledge systems.
Les Verts veulent développer de manière: The Greens want to significantly expand the broadcasting of CBC’s Indigenous programming “by ensuring that culturally relevant, Indigenous-led content is widely accessible and reflects the diverse Indigenous experiences and perspectives in Canada.” They also intend to increase CBC/Radio-Canada’s funding. Although they did not specify whether they would directly fund Indigenous media, they said they would increase funding for local news outlets.
Les Verts souhaitent enfin que les gouve: Finally, the Greens want First Nations governments to decide for themselves who is eligible for Indigenous procurement programs in order to prevent Indigenous identity fraud. To read the Green Party of Canada’s full election platform, please <l1>click here</l1>.
Le Bloc s’est engagé à établir une relat: The Bloc has committed to establishing a nation-to-nation relationship with Quebec’s First Nations and Inuit communities – and to ensuring that Ottawa respects UNDRIP. During the question period that followed the French-language debate, Yves-François Blanchet said First Nations should have a seat at the table in negotiations with the United States, stressing that Quebec respected their right to self-determination. In its election platform, the Bloc says the biggest obstacle to Indigenous self-determination is the Indian Act and that it would support an Indigenous-led initiative to repeal it.
M. Blanchet souhaite mettre fin à la dép: Mr. Blanchet wants to end Canada’s dependence on oil and gas and develop renewable energy sources in Quebec, in partnership with First Nations and Inuit.
Le Bloc s’efforcera de répondre aux appe: The Bloc will work to answer the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s calls to action. The party intends to invest in Indigenous cultures and languages, but its costed platform does not specify how much would be allocated to Indigenous groups. Its plan provides for $500 million a year for investments in culture in general. The party also promises to pressure the federal government to stop underfunding Indigenous police forces and to end boil-water advisories in communities.
Il allouerait en outre 650 M$ chaque ann: It would also allocate $650 million each year for four years to housing in Indigenous communities. You can consult the <l1>Bloc Québécois election platform here</l1> as well as its <l2>financial framework</l2>.
